turns.user:
I'm a Product Manager (IC6) at Meta in the Bay Area. Google reached out to me. I wasn't looking and I'm happy where I am, but after interviewing they've made me an offer for a Senior Product Manager role (L6) in San Francisco.

At Meta I make $240,000 base, a bonus of about $36,000, and about $250,000/yr in vesting RSUs, so roughly $526,000/yr. About $200,000 of RSUs would vest in my next 12 months if I stayed.

The offer:
- Base salary: $260,000
- Target annual bonus: 20% of base ($52,000)
- New-hire RSUs: $1,340,000, vesting over 4 years
- Sign-on bonus: $200,000

The job posting listed a base salary range of $183,000 to $271,000.

What the recruiter told me:
- Google gives annual equity refresh grants that stack over time, since each one vests over several years. The recruiter was clear that refreshes aren't guaranteed.

Compensation matters a lot to me. Is this a good offer? Should I accept it, negotiate, or walk away? If I negotiate, what exactly should I ask for, and how much?
turns.reply:
## Bottom line

**This is already a strong L6 PM offer. I would not walk away on compensation grounds. I would negotiate once, professionally, and would likely accept if the role/team is at least as attractive as Meta.**

My recommended counter:

- **Base:** $271,000  
- **New-hire RSUs:** ask for **$1.6 million**, aiming to land around **$1.5 million**
- **Sign-on:** ask for **$250,000**, although this is the least important lever

If they will move only one component, prioritize **equity**, then base, then sign-on.

---

## 1. What the Google offer is actually worth

Ignoring stock-price changes, bonus over/underperformance, benefits, and future refreshers:

| Component | Four-year value |
|---|---:|
| Base: $260K × 4 | $1,040,000 |
| Target bonus: $52K × 4 | $208,000 |
| New-hire RSUs | $1,340,000 |
| Sign-on | $200,000 |
| **Total** | **$2,788,000** |
| **Average per year** | **$697,000** |

Without the one-time sign-on, the recurring four-year average is **$647,000**.

Your stated Meta run rate is approximately:

- $526,000 × 4 = **$2,104,000**
- Google premium = approximately **$684,000 over four years**

That is a meaningful premium—about **$171,000 per year averaged over four years**.

One caveat: you said only **$200,000 of Meta stock will vest in the next 12 months**, which implies your actual forward-one-year Meta compensation is closer to **$476,000**, not $526,000, unless a new refresh changes that. For the real comparison, build a quarter-by-quarter schedule of your existing Meta grants for the next four years.

---

## 2. Confirm the vesting schedule before deciding

“Vesting over four years” is not enough information.

Google new-hire grants are commonly reported as front-loaded—often approximately **38% / 32% / 20% / 10%**—but you should not assume that applies to your grant. Get the exact percentages and vesting dates in writing. ([thesimplemoney.com](https://thesimplemoney.com/employers/google/gsu-grants-and-vesting-schedule?utm_source=openai))

If yours is 38/32/20/10, your compensation would look approximately like this:

| Year | Base + target bonus | New-hire RSUs | Sign-on | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | $312,000 | $509,200 | $200,000 | **$1,021,200** |
| 2 | $312,000 | $428,800 | — | **$740,800** |
| 3 | $312,000 | $268,000 | — | **$580,000** |
| 4 | $312,000 | $134,000 | — | **$446,000** |

That means:

- Years 1–3 are excellent.
- Year 4 falls below your current $526,000 Meta run rate unless refresh grants fill the gap.
- The headline “$1.34 million over four years” should not be mentally treated as $335,000 every year unless the grant actually vests 25% annually.

Refreshes are real elements of Google’s annual compensation process, but Google says their amounts depend on factors such as performance, role, location, modeled recommendations, and management discretion. They therefore should be treated as potential upside—not guaranteed compensation. ([services.google.com](https://services.google.com/fh/files/blogs/pay_equity_info_sheet.pdf?utm_source=openai))

---

## 3. Is it competitive for Google L6?

Yes.

Your $260,000 base is:

- $11,000 below the posting maximum of $271,000
- About **88% of the way from the bottom to the top of the posted range**

Recent self-reported compensation data puts Bay Area Google L6 PM median total compensation at approximately **$606,000**, though such data mixes new hires and existing employees and should be treated as directional. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area?utm_source=openai))

Another recent analysis of self-reported U.S. Google PM data found an L6 median around $514,000 and a 90th percentile around $671,000, again mixing offers and incumbent compensation. ([aakashg.com](https://www.aakashg.com/google-pm-job-offer/?utm_source=openai))

Your offer’s:

- **$647,000 average excluding sign-on**
- **$697,000 average including sign-on**
- exceptionally strong first two years if front-loaded

…makes it a strong package, not a lowball.

The $200,000 sign-on also exactly replaces the approximately $200,000 of Meta equity you say you would forfeit over the next 12 months. So Google has already recognized your immediate walk-away cost.

---

## 4. What I would negotiate

### Recommended opening ask

I would ask for:

> **$271,000 base, $1.6 million in new-hire equity, and $250,000 sign-on.**

That is an anchor, not necessarily your expected outcome.

A very good negotiated result would be something like:

- **$265,000–$271,000 base**
- **$1.45–$1.55 million equity**
- **$200,000–$250,000 sign-on**

### Why those amounts?

#### Base: ask for $271,000

It is the top of the disclosed range, and only $11,000 above the current offer. Because base also raises the target bonus, moving from $260,000 to $271,000 adds:

- $11,000 annual salary
- $2,200 annual target bonus
- About **$52,800 over four years**

That is modest relative to the whole package, but recurring and comparatively low-risk.

#### Equity: ask for $1.6 million

This is the most valuable negotiable lever. It is a roughly 19% increase from $1.34 million, leaving room to settle at $1.5 million.

The justification is not merely “market data.” It is:

- You are happy at Meta and were not conducting a job search.
- You are taking execution, team, performance-calibration, and promotion risk.
- Refreshes are expressly not guaranteed.
- A front-loaded new-hire grant may create a substantial year-four cliff.
- The guaranteed package must therefore stand on its own.

#### Sign-on: ask for $250,000

The existing $200,000 already makes you whole for the stated next-12-month Meta vesting, so this is the weakest part of the counter. Nevertheless, an additional $50,000 is a reasonable switching premium.

If the recruiter indicates the sign-on is already exceptional or capped, give this up before equity.

---

## 5. Suggested exact wording

You could send this:

> I’m genuinely excited about the team and the opportunity. At the same time, I’m happy at Meta and wasn’t actively looking, so the decision requires a meaningful premium to justify the switching risk.  
>  
> The offer is strong, and I appreciate the $200K sign-on offsetting the equity I would leave behind. My main concern is the longer-term guaranteed compensation, particularly because refresh grants aren’t guaranteed and the new-hire equity may be front-loaded.  
>  
> If Google could bring the package to **$271K base, $1.6M in new-hire equity, and $250K sign-on**, I would be in a position to make the decision quickly. My highest priority is the equity component if there is limited flexibility across all three areas.  
>  
> Could you take that back to the compensation team?

Only use “make the decision quickly” rather than “I will sign immediately” unless you truly are ready to commit.

If they ask what one change would close you, say:

> The most important change would be increasing the equity grant to **$1.5 million or better**.

---

## 6. Questions to get answered in writing

Before accepting, ask for:

1. **Exact new-hire RSU vesting percentages by year and vesting frequency.**
2. **When the share count is determined** and what happens if Alphabet’s price moves before the grant date.
3. **Expected first vest date**, especially whether starting after a certain date delays a quarterly vest.
4. **Sign-on payment timing and repayment/clawback terms.**
5. Whether the sign-on repayment is prorated and whether repayment is based on the **gross or net** amount.
6. **When you first become eligible for an equity refresh.**
7. How annual bonus is prorated in the first year.
8. Whether any upcoming compensation-review cutoff makes your start date important.
9. Whether the position is definitively **L6**, and whether the team’s scope gives you a credible L7 path.
10. Office attendance, location designation and whether San Francisco versus another Bay Area office affects compensation.

Do not assign a definite dollar value to future refreshes. If you want to model them, create both:

- **Floor case:** zero refreshes
- **Expected case:** estimated refreshes based on recruiter guidance
- **Upside case:** strong-performance refreshes

Make the decision primarily on the floor case.

---

## 7. Accept, negotiate, or walk?

### My recommendation: **Negotiate, then probably accept**

I would accept after negotiating if:

- You like the manager, team and product scope.
- The level is appropriate.
- The exact vesting schedule is understood.
- You are comfortable potentially changing jobs again around year three or four if refreshes do not materialize.
- There is no unusually harsh sign-on clawback.

I would stay at Meta if:

- You materially prefer your current manager, product or promotion trajectory.
- You believe your Meta equity vesting or refresh outlook is understated by the $526,000 figure.
- Google’s role is riskier, narrower or less promotable.
- You value remaining at Meta enough that a roughly $170,000 annual four-year premium is not sufficient.

I would **not walk merely because Google refuses the counter**. The existing offer is already compelling. Given that you were not looking, however, negotiating once is entirely appropriate—and you have enough leverage to make a firm, specific ask.
